title: Bowman links bank capital rules to Treasury dealing and community lending
bank: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
summary: Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman described two distinct ways regulation could affect markets. A leverage requirement that binds at a large bank can make the balance sheet used by its Treasury dealer expensive, even for positions with little credit risk. At a community bank, the cost of meeting a complex set of rules or crossing a fixed size threshold can affect decisions about expansion, mergers and credit provision. In her 7 January remarks, the change to the large-bank leverage rule had already been made, whereas the change to the community-bank leverage ratio was still a proposal. Bowman gave no estimate of observed changes in Treasury liquidity or bank lending under either measure. Her guidance concerned supervision and capital requirements, with no indication of her preferred federal funds rate.

For large institutions, Bowman presented the modified enhanced supplementary leverage ratio as a backstop to risk-based capital requirements. A leverage ratio measures exposures without weighting them by their individual risk. When it sets the binding constraint, even holding or financing lower-risk assets uses scarce balance sheet. The proposed mechanism for markets is that greater capacity at the broker-dealers affiliated with large banks could improve Treasury intermediation, particularly when customers want to sell and dealers must carry inventory. The private response matters. A dealer whose leverage constraint is already slack, or whose internal risk limits or funding costs set a tighter constraint, has less reason to expand. The speech contains neither trading data nor a change in Treasury yields attributable to the rule.

For eligible community banks choosing the simpler capital regime, Bowman supported reducing the required leverage ratio from 9% to 8%, the statutory minimum she identified. Under that option a bank meets one leverage requirement in place of the risk-based measures built for larger banks. The one-percentage-point change would therefore apply to participants in that regime if finalised. It cannot be applied across every community bank as a measure of capital freed for lending. A firm holding a sizeable voluntary buffer might continue to do so. Another bank might use greater flexibility to change its funding or enter the simplified regime. Bowman saw value in wider participation, but reported no change in loan approvals, borrowing rates or capital levels resulting from this proposal.

Supervision could also affect the cost and timing of banking activity without changing a numerical requirement. Bowman said the Fed had adjusted the ratings framework for large financial institutions so that one supervisory component would carry less disproportionate weight in a firm's overall status. For the separate CAMELS system used in bank examinations, she described work on how management is assessed and how findings are escalated. Ratings can affect deposit insurance costs, access to favourable application treatment and the cost of liquidity funding. A formal matter requiring attention leads to remediation. A nonbinding observation can bring an emerging issue to management early. A fall in formal findings after this change could reflect a different threshold for classification even if underlying loan quality remained the same.

The proposed thresholds raise a distinct question about incentives to grow. Bowman cited the $10 billion community-bank and $100 billion large-bank cut-offs as examples of fixed asset levels. An institution can cross a nominal boundary after years of inflation and economic growth without changing its business mix. She suggested considering nominal GDP indexation and, separately, the use of measures of risk and business model. Some thresholds have statutory origins and would involve Congress. She also favoured a distinct supervisory approach for community banks and a review of reporting costs and merger application delays. The speech made no change to either dollar cut-off. The historical comparison of banks immediately above and below a threshold should retain the rule actually in force.

Bowman used Silicon Valley Bank to explain her priorities. In her assessment, the breadth of previous examinations had drawn attention away from interest-rate and liquidity exposures. The October 2025 operating principles instructed staff to identify material risks and seek remediation earlier. She also reported removal of reputational risk from supervision and rescission of climate guidance, arguing that ordinary risk management already covered relevant financial exposures. This is her account of the trade-off in examiner time. Evaluating the change would require evidence that examiners detect and remedy significant weaknesses earlier, as well as evidence about problems that an altered examination might miss.

Several administrative changes affect how that evidence can be interpreted. The Fed was reviewing overlap with other bank supervisors, while reserving its own review when supporting documents were unavailable or inadequate. Bowman described work on the definition of unsafe practices, stress-test transparency, confidential supervisory information and more predictable application timetables. One manual for supervision of the largest firms had been published, with others to follow. None of these announcements measures a relaxation of standards for a specific institution. For a macro researcher, implementation dates, eligibility and the identity of a bank's binding constraint are more informative than counting the number of reforms announced in one speech.

questions.question: Did dealer balance-sheet capacity or Treasury market liquidity actually respond to the leverage-rule change?
questions.detail: Compare bank-affiliated dealers with different pre-change leverage headroom before and after the operative date. Track inventories, financing volumes, bid–ask spreads and the price impact of customer sales, particularly around heavy issuance or quarter-end. Control for Treasury supply, volatility and monetary operations. If supervisors' rule was rarely binding, larger inventories might instead reflect risk appetite or client flows, and narrower spreads need not identify the reform's effect.

questions.question: Would the proposed community-bank ratio change increase credit availability or chiefly alter which banks elect the simplified regime?
questions.detail: Separate proposal, finalisation and implementation dates, then compare eligible banks by prior capital buffers and participation. Observe entry into the regime, distributions, loan approvals and terms for similar borrowers. The one-percentage-point threshold change is an input. Its credit effect depends on capital buffers, eligible borrowers and loan demand. An increase in lending at participants alone could reflect the type of bank that chose to enter.

questions.question: Can examiners concentrate on material risks while still detecting future losses early?
questions.detail: Measure the time between an identifiable funding or asset-quality deterioration, a supervisory response and remediation, allowing for the reclassification of findings into informal observations. Compare subsequent losses and liquidity stress at institutions with comparable initial risk and different supervisors. Falling counts of formal findings or shorter application times would document procedural change, but would give little information on their own about the accuracy of risk assessment.
